findings.title: Annual revenue comparison does not establish the central affordability conclusion
findings.source_claim: Section 3.2 (p.4) says estimated data costs above annual revenue for three firms make compensation financially infeasible, then more tentatively suggests only the wealthiest organizations could afford it.
findings.suspect_step: D>R -> inability to pay D; no assumption bounds available funds by R
findings.check_type: analytic countermodel plus exact rational arithmetic
assumption_checks: Cost follows original wage/speed and integer corpus size
No royalties, discounted labor or new finance used
Original text states no zero-cash or revenue-only funding constraint
Data are a one-time acquisition; Section 5 explicitly considers reuse; no mandatory annual repurchase imposed.
findings.counterevidence: D/R is a defensible descriptive burden metric. The broader population statement is qualified. The hypothetical itself is wealthy and does not refute it. Royalties and amortization are explicitly discussed; neither rescues the categorical inference because full immediate payment is feasible in the countermodel.
findings.dependency: Section3.2 establishes prominent practical takeaway repeated in introduction, Section4 and Section4.3
findings.impact: The statistic does not establish the company-level infeasibility conclusion used in the introduction and Sections 4/4.3. No named company's finances or population-level wealth claim are empirically refuted.

repair.statement: Use D/R as descriptive cost-to-revenue scale, without inferring ability to finance
repair.verification: Verified logical narrowing and displayed threshold counts only; original affordability conclusion not restored; historical input accuracy unverified.
